newsitem.title: ICELAND: Flood threat from Iceland glacier recedes for now.
newsitem.headline: Flood threat from Iceland glacier recedes for now.

text.p: Scientists on Thursday said the immediate threat of massive flooding from a lake of volcanic melt water building up under Europe's largest glacier in southern Iceland has receded.

But experts surveying the volcanic eruptions under the huge Vatnajokull glacier that are filling the Grimsvotn subglacial lake with water say the ice-cap will eventually crack, pouring torrents of water across Iceland's southern plains.

"There is no doubt the flood will occur but the change in activity makes the timing more uncertain. I still think the most likely option is that it will begin in days," said geophysicist Magnus Tumi Gudmundsson, head of aerial monitoring.
Since the volcano began erupting last week Iceland has been expecting the glacier's icecap to give way any day under the strain of the lake's rising water levels.
Although the volcano continues to rumble, pouring out huge clouds of gas and steam, and the lake's water levels are still rising, scientists said the activity has slowed.

"The lake rose some 80 metres (265 feet) in the first four days of the eruption but we believe it's increased perhaps by 15 metres in the five days since," said Gudmundsson. "It has slowed dramatically."
"If melting had continued at the initial rate the flood would have started by now," he told Reuters.

When the glacier's icecap cracks scientists estimate a tidal wave of water will flood the vast, uninhabited black sand plain that surrounds the desolate glacier, located about 250 kms (150 miles) east of Reykjavik.

The area, now an emergency zone, is deserted except for journalists and government workers trying to protect the country's one coastal ring road, which passes through a small settlement southwest of the glacier.

A break in heavy, black skies on Wednesday allowed several aircraft to fly over the glacier to permit visual monitoring of the eruption site for the first time in four days but on Thursday the clouds returned and snow was forecast.
University of Iceland seismologist, Bryndis Brandsdottir, said Wednesday's flights had showed the volcano was continuing to rumble at a steady rate.

"There is constant tremor activity at the eruption site but the pulsating bursts we saw a few days ago are becoming less frequent," Brandsdottir told Reuters. "The eruption is ongoing but stabilised."
"The longer we have to wait, the larger the floods will be," said Gudmundsson. "That also depends on the rate of melting of the ice. We really cannot make any sensible predictions on the flood."

Government estimates put the cost of the expected flood in a worst-case scenario at 1.5 billion Icelandic crowns ($22 million), assuming all the bridges, roads and power lines in the area are wiped out.
But the actual cost to public finances would be limited. Most of the cost would be borne by an insurance fund set up by the government after a massive volcanic eruption in 1973.
